svg.title: Protected areas. A request for a path a "protect" rule covers, or a page whose application asks with the header X-Request-Shield-Access naming an area: an address the rule lets in (the office's range) goes through without a password; a valid area cookie goes through; anything else gets the shield's own small form instead of the page. The form takes a password (written in the rule file only as a hash) or a code. A code is issued by the application, the command line or the dashboard: it is valid for a time, for a number of uses, and has a note; the store keeps only its hash. A right password or code sets a signed cookie for that area for some hours and sends the visitor on to the page; a code in a link is taken out of the address before anything is logged. Wrong attempts count against a budget of their own: past it, a pause and the browser check, and, with bans, a ban. Other parts of the website are not touched: restrict still keeps areas for certain addresses only.

Passwords
chosen by people: password_hash() (bcrypt/argon2)
bin/request-shield password → the line to paste
changed: every cookie of the area ends
Parts of a website by address
exists: restrict <paths> to <ranges> (403)
new: … or a password, … at times (Mon–Fri 8–18)
Like .htaccess Basic Auth, but: hashes only, codes that end or are used up, issued by the application,
a form instead of the browser's dialog, brute force counted and banned, every refusal in the live view.
The site can ask too: X-Request-Shield-Access: A-PREVIEW (the CMS marks a page protected) -- the area only, never a password.
Not a replacement for the application's own users and roles: for areas without a login of their own.
